name: Dimple creation surgery (dimpleplasty)

card.summary: Dimple creation surgery, or dimpleplasty, is a minor cosmetic procedure that creates cheek dimples that appear when smiling, aiming at a more youthful, charming smile.
card.note: Surgical complications near the facial nerve and parotid duct are described; people prone to keloids are cautioned.

quick.overview:
Dimpleplasty surgically creates the small cheek indentations that appear when a person smiles. A 2025 review says natural dimples occur in roughly 30% of faces, and the procedure recreates them.

People seek it because dimples are widely seen as attractive and youthful; Wikipedia notes they are associated with beauty and, in Chinese culture, good luck.
quick.how: In the technique described in the review, a surgeon makes a small intraoral incision of about 5 mm, treats part of the cheek muscle and anchors skin to muscle so a dimple forms immediately and softens with healing. Placement relies on landmarks such as the Khoo Boo-Chai point.
quick.risks: Reported complications include swelling, hematoma and infection; surgeons must account for anatomy including Stenson's duct and facial nerve branches. People with a tendency to keloid scarring are cautioned.

lead: Dimple creation surgery, or dimpleplasty, is a minor cosmetic procedure that creates the small cheek indentations that appear when a person smiles. A 2025 review in Facial Plastic Surgery describes natural dimples as occurring in roughly 30% of faces and traces the technique through successive refinements since 1962 toward smaller incisions and precise fixation of skin to muscle.[1] People seek it because dimples are widely associated with youth, charm and a cheerful smile; Wikipedia notes that they are regarded as attractive in many cultures and as a good-luck sign in Chinese culture.[7]

In the commonly described approach, a surgeon works from inside the mouth and anchors the cheek skin to the underlying muscle so that a dent forms when the muscle moves. The result is a dynamic dimple that shows on smiling rather than a fixed pit. Reviews and case series describe several variants, from suture-only methods to punch excision, and the literature on placement has grown since the 2010s.[1][3][12]

The published evidence consists of narrative reviews, technique notes, case series and measurement studies of natural dimples. The largest series reports 2,048 patients treated at one clinic over four years.[11] The topic is occasionally raised on looksmax.org, where members give mixed opinions on how much a dimple changes overall looks.[6]

chain: Small incision creates a skin-to-muscle attachment in the cheek
angle.text: Dimpleplasty adds cheek dimples that show on smiling, for people who want that feature.

infobox: Usually intraoral, small incision (about 5 mm in a 2025 review)[1]
A dynamic dimple that shows on smiling

paras: Dimpleplasty aims to reproduce a natural cheek dimple, which is a dynamic indentation in mobile skin. One proposed anatomical explanation for natural dimples is a double or bifid zygomaticus major muscle that splits into two bundles, one inserting above and one below the corner of the mouth; other muscle variants and fibrous bands are also discussed.[7][1] Natural dimples are most often found on both cheeks or on one side only, depending on the population studied.[1][8]

The 2025 review in Facial Plastic Surgery describes a procedure built around a 5-mm intraoral incision, selective fenestration of part of the cheek muscle and dermomuscular plication, producing an immediate dimple that softens as swelling settles. The authors stress knowledge of the zygomaticus major, orbicularis oculi bands, Stenson's (parotid) duct and the buccal branches of the facial nerve, mention bipolar cautery for hemostasis and a short course of oral antibiotics, and report that healthy adults with realistic expectations are the usual candidates.[1]

A 2026 narrative review in the Journal of Maxillofacial and Oral Surgery proposes a classification of techniques by invasiveness, method and approach, and covers punch excision, suture-based and minimally invasive options, as well as the psychological, social and ethical aspects of the procedure.[14]

A 2007 report from China described passing a monofilament nylon suture through the dermis and buccinator muscle with a syringe needle to form a sling, in 56 dimples in 36 women; the authors described patient satisfaction with shape, no hematoma or infection and a return to work after about two days.[12] A 2010 paper from India described an open technique designed to mirror the anatomy of a natural dimple, offered as an alternative to blind coring or transcutaneous sutures.[12]

In 2012 Lari and Panse reported 100 dimple creations under local anesthesia as a day-care procedure, scraping the dermis free of mucomuscular attachments and placing a transcutaneous bolster stitch without excising tissue; they reported high satisfaction including at long follow-up.[12] A 2015 Egyptian series used an intraoral stab incision and a Prolene suture to fix the dermis to the buccinator, reporting satisfaction in about 86% of 74 patients, fading or loss of the dimple in 14 cases and infection in five.[12] A 2015 case series of 23 women using a suturing technique reported minor swelling and hematoma in four cases and infection in two, with most subjects satisfied.[9]

A 2025 case report described a 35-year-old man who developed a single dimple after a facial thread lift; the authors suggested thread lifting might be explored as a less invasive way to create dimples and called for further study.[12] Chin dimples have also been addressed surgically in single-patient reports.[13]

sections.h: Placement and the Khoo Boo-Chai point
paras: Wikipedia credits the Singaporean surgeon Khoo Boo-Chai with describing, in 1962, a cheek location on the line between the corner of the mouth and the outer corner of the eye, now called the KBC point and still the standard reference.[7][4] Later studies of natural dimples have asked whether that point matches real anatomy. A 2018 study examined 1,194 people, included 216 with 336 natural dimples and sorted faces into mesoprosopic, euryprosopic and leptoprosopic forms; it found that 54.8 percent of dimples were not on the KBC point and proposed landmarks by face shape.[4]

An Indian study of 1,462 people found natural dimples in 121; unilateral dimples (72.9%) outnumbered bilateral, 60.7% of dimples sat at the KBC point and the rest were a mean of 9.86 mm anterior to it.[8] A 2025 observational study used 3D-scanned faces and a panel of raters to compare three landmark positions, reporting that the KBC point received the highest overall rating while other positions suited particular facial proportions.[5][13] Researchers have also described AI-assisted 3D smile simulation as a developing tool for planning.[1]

The 2025 review characterises dimpleplasty as a low-risk procedure with high patient satisfaction when patients are selected carefully, and advises caution in people with a tendency to form keloid scars.[1] Reported complications in series include swelling, hematoma, infection, asymmetry and a dimple that fades or is too shallow or too deep.[9][12]

A 2020 paper in Archives of Plastic Surgery analysed 2,048 patients treated between April 2010 and June 2014. It found that 159 patients (7.7%) required reoperation, mainly for undercorrection (49.0%) and disappearance of the dimple (38.9%), with overcorrection in 5.6%; five patients had stitches removed for infection and the authors saw no hyperpigmentation or foreign-body reactions.[11] A 2014 case report described a chronic discharging nodule in the buccal mucosa, an actinomycotic sinus, after cheek dimple creation, treated by complete excision.[13] Because the cheek contains the parotid duct and facial nerve branches, authors emphasise anatomical knowledge in planning.[1]

Interest in artificial dimples predates surgery. Wikipedia reports that a device called the Dolly Dimpler was advertised in Photoplay in 1926, and that in 1936 Isabella Gilbert invented the Dimple Maker, a face brace that pressed dents into the cheeks.[7] Surgical creation became available from the 1960s and, per Wikipedia, was widely used in the 21st century; it cites a 2017 Independent report describing a rise in cosmetic dimple surgery among millennials.[7]

Dimples carry cultural associations of beauty and youth, noted in an 1866 magazine article, and of luck in Chinese culture, where children born with them are believed to be cheerful.[7] Haitian mothers are reported to press small indents into newborns' cheeks in the hope of forming dimples.[7]

Dimpleplasty is a minor topic in looksmaxxing communities. In a looksmax.org thread asking about the surgery, one reply argues that dimples do not change a person's overall rating and are comparable to a niche feature such as glasses on an already attractive man, while another reply jokes about their appeal.[6]

Human research is limited to narrative reviews and technique notes (2012, 2025, 2026),[2][1][3] case series of 23, 36, 74 and 100 patients,[9][12] a retrospective review of 2,048 patients,[11] and measurement studies of natural dimples.[4][8][5] These report high satisfaction, minor complications and a reoperation rate of 7.7% in the largest series. No randomized trial or study of how dimple creation changes rated attractiveness is described.

timeline.event: The Dolly Dimpler, a dimple-making device, is advertised in Photoplay.[7]
Isabella Gilbert invents the Dimple Maker, a cheek-pressing face brace.[7]
Surgeon Khoo Boo-Chai describes the cheek reference point later called the KBC point.[7][1]
A suture-sling technique using the buccinator muscle is reported in 36 women.[12]
A 100-case series and a literature review with a technique note are published.[12][14]
A 23-patient suturing series and a 74-patient intraoral series are reported.[9][12]
The Independent reports a rise in cosmetic dimple surgery among millennials, per Wikipedia.[7]
A study of 1,194 people finds 54.8% of natural dimples are off the KBC point.[4]
A series of 2,048 patients reports a 7.7% reoperation rate.[11]
A Facial Plastic Surgery review and a 3D-model landmark study are published.[1][5]

lore.intro: Dimpleplasty is discussed only occasionally on looksmax.org, where opinions about its effect on overall looks are mixed.[6]

claims.claim: Dimples do not improve overall looks
claims.believers: One forum reply says dimples are a niche feature and that 'awwww he has dimples' does not change a person's rating.[6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and a prevalence study describe dimples as regarded as attractive and as a sign of beauty, but no study has measured how surgical dimples change rated attractiveness.[7][8]

claims.claim: A dimple makes the smile look more youthful and cheerful
claims.believers: Practitioners and patients cite charm and youthfulness as reasons for the surgery.[1][7]
claims.experts: Surgeons in a 2020 series state that cheek dimples can make a smile appear more cheerful; satisfaction is reported in case series without controlled comparison.[11][12]

claims.claim: The KBC point is the right place for every face
claims.believers: Many surgeons have used the 1962 landmark as the standard.[4]
claims.experts: A 2018 study found 54.8% of natural dimples off the KBC point, while a 2025 3D-model panel rated the KBC point highest overall with other points suiting some proportions.[4][5]

claims.believers: Surgeons describe an immediate dimple that softens with healing.[1]
claims.experts: Series report that some dimples fade or disappear and that 7.7% of one large series needed reoperation, mainly for undercorrection or disappearance.[11][12]

claims.claim: A thread lift can create a dimple
claims.believers: The authors of a 2025 case report suggest it as a less invasive route.[12]
claims.experts: Only a single case report exists and its authors call for more study of safety and satisfaction.[12]
